query: For refractory high-entropy alloys intended for structural use under extreme-temperature conditions, what single intervention could improve high-temperature oxygen resistance? State one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts the improvement relative to the untreated alloy, defines the temperature, atmosphere, and exposure conditions under which it should work, cites supporting prior evidence, and proposes an experiment with a clear result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Adding a minor alloying addition of Cr (in combination with available Ta) to a refractory high‐entropy alloy will promote the in situ formation of a dense CrTaO4-based oxide scale at high temperatures, thereby enhancing the alloy’s oxygen resistance.
generation.material_initial_state: A refractory high‐entropy alloy (RHEA) that, without targeted composition adjustment, forms a less-protective oxide scale under high-temperature oxidation (e.g., exhibiting exponential weight gain at ~1000 °C).
generation.intervention: Modify the alloy composition by introducing a controlled minor addition of Cr (with Ta present) to favor the formation of a continuous, adherent CrTaO4 oxide scale.
generation.conditions: Isothermal oxidation in an air atmosphere at approximately 1100 °C for up to 200 hours.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of a continuous, dense CrTaO4-based oxide layer on the alloy surface.
generation.mechanism: The Cr addition reacts with the available Ta during high-temperature exposure to form a protective CrTaO4 oxide that limits oxygen diffusion into the bulk alloy, thereby reducing oxidation kinetics compared to alloys that do not form this scale.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the untreated alloy, the modified RHEA will exhibit a significantly lower weight gain (indicative of reduced oxidation) and a more protective oxide morphology under the specified conditions.
generation.baseline: Untreated RHEAs have shown exponential oxidation behavior at 1000 °C with a non-dense external oxide layer, leading to higher mass gains over prolonged exposures.
generation.boundary: The beneficial effect is expected only when the overall alloy chemistry provides sufficient Ta and other supporting elements for CrTaO4 formation; the intervention may not work under cyclic oxidation or in atmospheres with additional reactive species.
generation.uncertainty: The precise magnitude of improvement in weight gain reduction and the long-term stability of the protective oxide scale under variable operational conditions remain to be quantitatively established.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of refractory high-entropy alloys: one with the standard composition (without the minor Cr addition) and one with the controlled Cr addition (and sufficient Ta) hypothesized to form CrTaO4. Subject both alloy sets to isothermal oxidation at 1100 °C in air for 200 hours. Characterize the oxide scale morphology using SEM/EDS and measure the weight gain over time.
measurements: Total mass gain (mg/cm2) over the exposure period.
Oxide scale thickness and continuity via microscopy.
Phase identification of the oxide scale using XRD.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Cr-added alloy does not show a statistically significant reduction in weight gain and fails to develop a continuous, predominantly CrTaO4-based oxide scale compared to the untreated alloy under identical oxidation conditions, then the hypothesis will be considered falsified.

cited_evidence.text:
An oxidation resistant refractory high entropy alloy protected by CrTaO4-based oxide

Abstract: AbstractAlthough refractory high entropy alloys (RHEAs) have shown potentials to be developed as structural materials for elevated temperature applications, most of the reported oxidation behaviours of RHEA were associated with short term exposures for only up to 48 hours, and there is a lack of understanding on the oxidation mechanism of any RHEA to-date. In this work, by using thermogravimetric analysis, isothermal oxidation was conducted on a novel RHEA at 1000 °C and 1100 °C for up to 200 hours, which is an unprecedented testing duration. The external oxide layer strongly influenced the weight gain behaviours, and it consisted of CrTaO4-based oxide with some dispersion of Al2O3 and Cr2O3. At 1000 °C, the inability to form dense CrTaO4-based oxide layer resulted an exponential dependence of weight gain throughout 200 hours.
